title: One Church, twenty-four churches
hook: the Latin Church and the Eastern Catholic churches, all in communion with Rome

segments.voice: Yesterday, the close of the days on Mary, at a wedding where the wine ran out. Your line was she points to him. Did you do the one thing you chose? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

A few streets from a parish with pews and a kneeler in every row, there's another church. Golden domes. Inside, a wall of icons, a cloud of incense, and a priest with a beard. Candles burn in front of the icons. The bulletin is in English and Ukrainian. A Catholic from the first parish walks in, a little unsure, and asks the woman at the door whether this is an Orthodox church. She smiles, because she gets asked that a lot. No, she says. We're Catholic. We just aren't Roman. Today's word is the little Latin phrase that makes that possible.
screen: `DOMES, ICONS, INCENSE.` → `IS THIS ORTHODOX?` → `CATHOLIC, JUST NOT ROMAN.`

segments.voice: First, the phrase. Sui iuris is Latin for of its own law. The Code of Canons of the Eastern Churches uses it for a church with its own hierarchy, recognized as self-governing by the Church's highest authority. Its own bishops, and sometimes its own patriarch. Its own law. Its own liturgy, calendar, saints and ways of praying. And all of it in full communion with the bishop of Rome. Second, the families. The Catechism names the great liturgical traditions in use in the Church: the Latin, and then the Byzantine, the Alexandrian or Coptic, the Syriac, the Armenian, the Maronite and the Chaldean. Out of those traditions come the Eastern Catholic churches: Ukrainians and Melkites, Maronites in Lebanon, Syro-Malabar Catholics in India, Chaldeans from Iraq, Copts and Ethiopians and Armenians, and more. Today's title counts them up. Third, equal dignity. The Second Vatican Council, in its decree on the Eastern churches, said these churches are of equal dignity, and that none of them outranks another because of its rite. The Latin Church sits at that table as one church among them, not the owner of the house. The Council asked the Eastern churches to keep their own traditions whole, not trade them for Latin ones. Fourth, the picture. Pope John Paul the Second wrote that the Church must breathe with both its lungs, East and West. Catholic doesn't only mean Roman. So for a Latin Catholic, the parish with the domes down the street isn't a stranger's church. It belongs to the same communion.
screen: `SUI IURIS: OF ITS OWN LAW.` · `BYZANTINE, COPTIC, SYRIAC, ARMENIAN...` · `EQUAL DIGNITY, ONE COMMUNION.` · `BREATHING WITH BOTH LUNGS.` · then, large: `ONE CHURCH, MANY CHURCHES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find the Eastern Catholic church nearest you, starting in your mind. Settle, and breathe. Picture your town or city from above. Somewhere in it, or not far off, there may be a church whose people pray in Arabic, or Ukrainian, or Malayalam, or Syriac, and who are Catholic too. You don't need to know where yet. Just hold them as part of the same family, for a few breaths. If you pray, you can pray for them in any words you know. If you don't, simply let the map grow larger than it was this morning. After the bell, you might look one up. The bell holds the time.
Sui iuris. Of its own law: a church with its own hierarchy, liturgy and law, in full communion with Rome. Today's word.
Your line: one church, many churches. Today, look up the nearest Eastern Catholic parish, and read the name of the church it belongs to. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-seven.

howItsDone: Eastern Catholics belong to their own churches sui iuris, with their own bishops, liturgy and law, while in full communion with the pope; Latin Catholics may attend their liturgies, and in some cities Eastern Catholic parishes stand a few streets from Latin ones.

fork.setup: you lead an Eastern church in full communion with Rome. what does the Council ask you to do with your own liturgy and customs?
options: replace them with the Latin ones.
keep them whole, and return to them where they've been lost.
keep the liturgy but give up your own law.
fork.reveal: the decree on the Eastern churches asks them to keep their own rites and way of life, as churches of equal dignity.

original.note: Latin: of its own law, or in its own right.

trapdoor: what you thought: Catholic means Roman Catholic.
what it means: one Catholic Church made of a family of churches, each with its own law, liturgy and bishops, all in communion with Rome.
what a scholar hears: sui iuris in the Eastern code of canon law, the Catechism's list of liturgical traditions, and the Council's 'equal dignity' in Orientalium Ecclesiarum.
recall: a line from the Song of Songs

notes: The index title and hook give counts (twenty-four; twenty-three Eastern churches). Per the claims rule the voice does not state the count ('Today's title counts them up') and the script hook field drops it. Confirm the current official count before shipping the title.

The sample of Eastern Catholic churches (Ukrainian, Melkite, Maronite, Syro-Malabar, Chaldean, Coptic, Ethiopian, Armenian) is a sample, not a list; confirm names and the places attached (Lebanon, India, Iraq).
John Paul II's 'two lungs' image paraphrased (Ut Unum Sint 54 and elsewhere). Confirm.

Earlier drafts claimed the Latin Church is the largest, a Greek etymology for catholic, and a married priest in the hook; all cut under the claims rule. The hook keeps "the whole service is sung, start to finish" as a scene detail; confirm.
